./FAQ.md:952:<h3 name="posix4ever">
./FAQ.md:953:Can ripgrep replace grep?
./FAQ.md:954:</h3>
./FAQ.md:955:
./FAQ.md:956:Yes and no.
./FAQ.md:957:
./FAQ.md:958:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep
./FAQ.md:959:can be used in every instance grep can be used, in exactly the same way, for
./FAQ.md:960:the same use cases, with exactly the same bug-for-bug behavior," then no,
./FAQ.md:961:ripgrep trivially *cannot* replace grep. Moreover, ripgrep will *never* replace
./FAQ.md:962:grep.
./FAQ.md:963:
./FAQ.md:964:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep
./FAQ.md:965:can replace grep in some cases and not in other use cases," then yes, that is
./FAQ.md:966:indeed true!
./FAQ.md:967:
./FAQ.md:968:Let's go over some of those use cases in favor of ripgrep. Some of these may
./FAQ.md:969:not apply to you. That's OK. There may be other use cases not listed here that
./FAQ.md:970:do apply to you. That's OK too.
./FAQ.md:971:
./FAQ.md:972:(For all claims related to performance in the following words, see my
./FAQ.md:973:[blog post](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
./FAQ.md:974:introducing ripgrep.)
./FAQ.md:975:
./FAQ.md:976:* Are you frequently searching a repository of code? If so, ripgrep might be a
./FAQ.md:977:  good choice since there's likely a good chunk of your repository that you
./FAQ.md:978:  don't want to search. grep, can, of course, be made to filter files using
./FAQ.md:979:  recursive search, and if you don't mind writing out the requisite `--exclude`
./FAQ.md:980:  rules or writing wrapper scripts, then grep might be sufficient. (I'm not
./FAQ.md:981:  kidding, I myself did this with grep for almost a decade before writing
./FAQ.md:982:  ripgrep.) But if you instead enjoy having a search tool respect your
./FAQ.md:983:  `.gitignore`, then ripgrep might be perfect for you!
./FAQ.md:984:* Are you frequently searching non-ASCII text that is UTF-8 encoded? One of
./FAQ.md:985:  ripgrep's key features is that it can handle Unicode features in your
./FAQ.md:986:  patterns in a way that tends to be faster than GNU grep. Unicode features
./FAQ.md:987:  in ripgrep are enabled by default; there is no need to configure your locale
./FAQ.md:988:  settings to use ripgrep properly because ripgrep doesn't respect your locale
./FAQ.md:989:  settings.
./FAQ.md:990:* Do you need to search UTF-16 files and you don't want to bother explicitly
./FAQ.md:991:  transcoding them? Great. ripgrep does this for you automatically. No need
./FAQ.md:992:  to enable it.
./FAQ.md:993:* Do you need to search a large directory of large files? ripgrep uses
./FAQ.md:994:  parallelism by default, which tends to make it faster than a standard
./FAQ.md:995:  `grep -r` search. However, if you're OK writing the occasional
./FAQ.md:996:  `find ./ -print0 | xargs -P8 -0 grep` command, then maybe grep is good
./FAQ.md:997:  enough.
./FAQ.md:998:
./FAQ.md:999:Here are some cases where you might *not* want to use ripgrep. The same caveats
./FAQ.md:1000:for the previous section apply.
./FAQ.md:1001:
./FAQ.md:1002:* Are you writing portable shell scripts intended to work in a variety of
./FAQ.md:1003:  environments? Great, probably not a good idea to use ripgrep! ripgrep has
./FAQ.md:1004:  nowhere near the ubiquity of grep, so if you do use ripgrep, you might need
./FAQ.md:1005:  to futz with the installation process more than you would with grep.
./FAQ.md:1006:* Do you care about POSIX compatibility? If so, then you can't use ripgrep
./FAQ.md:1007:  because it never was, isn't and never will be POSIX compatible.
./FAQ.md:1008:* Do you hate tools that try to do something smart? If so, ripgrep is all about
./FAQ.md:1009:  being smart, so you might prefer to just stick with grep.
./FAQ.md:1010:* Is there a particular feature of grep you rely on that ripgrep either doesn't
./FAQ.md:1011:  have or never will have? If the former, file a bug report, maybe ripgrep can
./FAQ.md:1012:  do it! If the latter, well, then, just use grep.
./FAQ.md:1013:
./FAQ.md:1014:
./FAQ.md:1015:<h3 name="intentcountsforsomething">
./FAQ.md:1016:What does the "rip" in ripgrep mean?
./FAQ.md:1017:</h3>
./FAQ.md:1018:
./FAQ.md:1019:When I first started writing ripgrep, I called it `rep`, intending it to be a
./FAQ.md:1020:shorter variant of `grep`. Soon after, I renamed it to `xrep` since `rep`
./FAQ.md:1021:wasn't obvious enough of a name for my taste. And also because adding `x` to
./FAQ.md:1022:anything always makes it better, right?
./FAQ.md:1023:
./FAQ.md:1024:Before ripgrep's first public release, I decided that I didn't like `xrep`. I
./FAQ.md:1025:thought it was slightly awkward to type, and despite my previous praise of the
./FAQ.md:1026:letter `x`, I kind of thought it was pretty lame. Being someone who really
./FAQ.md:1027:likes Rust, I wanted to call it "rustgrep" or maybe "rgrep" for short. But I
./FAQ.md:1028:thought that was just as lame, and maybe a little too in-your-face. But I
./FAQ.md:1029:wanted to continue using `r` so I could at least pretend Rust had something to
./FAQ.md:1030:do with it.
./FAQ.md:1031:
./FAQ.md:1032:I spent a couple of days trying to think of very short words that began with
./FAQ.md:1033:the letter `r` that were even somewhat related to the task of searching. I
./FAQ.md:1034:don't remember how it popped into my head, but "rip" came up as something that
./FAQ.md:1035:meant "fast," as in, "to rip through your text." The fact that RIP is also
./FAQ.md:1036:an initialism for "Rest in Peace" (as in, "ripgrep kills grep") never really
./FAQ.md:1037:dawned on me. Perhaps the coincidence is too striking to believe that, but
./FAQ.md:1038:I didn't realize it until someone explicitly pointed it out to me after the
./FAQ.md:1039:initial public release. I admit that I found it mildly amusing, but if I had
./FAQ.md:1040:realized it myself before the public release, I probably would have pressed on
./FAQ.md:1041:and chose a different name. Alas, renaming things after a release is hard, so I
./FAQ.md:1042:decided to mush on.
./FAQ.md:1043:
./FAQ.md:1044:Given the fact that
./FAQ.md:1045:[ripgrep never was, is or will be a 100% drop-in replacement for
./FAQ.md:1046:grep](#posix4ever),
./FAQ.md:1047:ripgrep is neither actually a "grep killer" nor was it ever intended to be. It
./FAQ.md:1048:certainly does eat into some of its use cases, but that's nothing that other
./FAQ.md:1049:tools like ack or The Silver Searcher weren't already doing.
./FAQ.md:1050:

./GUIDE.md:1:## User Guide
./GUIDE.md:2:
./GUIDE.md:3:This guide is intended to give an elementary description of ripgrep and an
./GUIDE.md:4:overview of its capabilities. This guide assumes that ripgrep is
./GUIDE.md:5:[installed](README.md#installation)
./GUIDE.md:6:and that readers have passing familiarity with using command line tools. This
./GUIDE.md:7:also assumes a Unix-like system, although most commands are probably easily
./GUIDE.md:8:translatable to any command line shell environment.

./GUIDE.md:26:### Basics
./GUIDE.md:27:
./GUIDE.md:28:ripgrep is a command line tool that searches your files for patterns that
./GUIDE.md:29:you give it. ripgrep behaves as if reading each file line by line. If a line
./GUIDE.md:30:matches the pattern provided to ripgrep, then that line will be printed. If a
./GUIDE.md:31:line does not match the pattern, then the line is not printed.
./GUIDE.md:32:
./GUIDE.md:33:The best way to see how this works is with an example. To show an example, we
./GUIDE.md:34:need something to search. Let's try searching ripgrep's source code. First
./GUIDE.md:35:grab a ripgrep source archive from
./GUIDE.md:36:https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/archive/0.7.1.zip
./GUIDE.md:37:and extract it:
./GUIDE.md:38:
./GUIDE.md:39:```
./GUIDE.md:40:$ curl -LO https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/archive/0.7.1.zip
./GUIDE.md:41:$ unzip 0.7.1.zip
./GUIDE.md:42:$ cd ripgrep-0.7.1
./GUIDE.md:43:$ ls
./GUIDE.md:44:benchsuite  grep       tests         Cargo.toml       LICENSE-MIT
./GUIDE.md:45:ci          ignore     wincolor      CHANGELOG.md     README.md
./GUIDE.md:46:complete    pkg        appveyor.yml  compile          snapcraft.yaml
./GUIDE.md:47:doc         src        build.rs      COPYING          UNLICENSE
./GUIDE.md:48:globset     termcolor  Cargo.lock    HomebrewFormula
./GUIDE.md:49:```
./GUIDE.md:50:
./GUIDE.md:51:Let's try our first search by looking for all occurrences of the word `fast`
./GUIDE.md:52:in `README.md`:
./GUIDE.md:53:
./GUIDE.md:54:```
./GUIDE.md:55:$ rg fast README.md
./GUIDE.md:56:75:  faster than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement
./GUIDE.md:57:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast while
./GUIDE.md:58:119:### Is it really faster than everything else?
./GUIDE.md:59:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast because:
./GUIDE.md:60:129:  optimizations to make searching very fast.
./GUIDE.md:61:```
./GUIDE.md:62:
./GUIDE.md:63:(**Note:** If you see an error message from ripgrep saying that it didn't
./GUIDE.md:64:search any files, then re-run ripgrep with the `--debug` flag. One likely cause
./GUIDE.md:65:of this is that you have a `*` rule in a `$HOME/.gitignore` file.)
./GUIDE.md:66:
./GUIDE.md:67:So what happened here? ripgrep read the contents of `README.md`, and for each
./GUIDE.md:68:line that contained `fast`, ripgrep printed it to your terminal. ripgrep also
./GUIDE.md:69:included the line number for each line by default. If your terminal supports
./GUIDE.md:70:colors, then your output might actually look something like this screenshot:
./GUIDE.md:71:
./GUIDE.md:72:[![A screenshot of a sample search ripgrep](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/ripgrep-guide-sample.png)](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/ripgrep-guide-sample.png)
./GUIDE.md:73:
./GUIDE.md:74:In this example, we searched for something called a "literal" string. This
./GUIDE.md:75:means that our pattern was just some normal text that we asked ripgrep to
./GUIDE.md:76:find. But ripgrep supports the ability to specify patterns via [regular
./GUIDE.md:77:expressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression). As an example,
./GUIDE.md:78:what if we wanted to find all lines have a word that contains `fast` followed
./GUIDE.md:79:by some number of other letters?
./GUIDE.md:80:
./GUIDE.md:81:```
./GUIDE.md:82:$ rg 'fast\w+' README.md
./GUIDE.md:83:75:  faster than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement
./GUIDE.md:84:119:### Is it really faster than everything else?
./GUIDE.md:85:```
./GUIDE.md:86:
./GUIDE.md:87:In this example, we used the pattern `fast\w+`. This pattern tells ripgrep to
./GUIDE.md:88:look for any lines containing the letters `fast` followed by *one or more*
./GUIDE.md:89:word-like characters. Namely, `\w` matches characters that compose words (like
./GUIDE.md:90:`a` and `L` but unlike `.` and ` `). The `+` after the `\w` means, "match the
./GUIDE.md:91:previous pattern one or more times." This means that the word `fast` won't
./GUIDE.md:92:match because there are no word characters following the final `t`. But a word
./GUIDE.md:93:like `faster` will. `faste` would also match!
./GUIDE.md:94:
./GUIDE.md:95:Here's a different variation on this same theme:
./GUIDE.md:96:
./GUIDE.md:97:```
./GUIDE.md:98:$ rg 'fast\w*' README.md
./GUIDE.md:99:75:  faster than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement
./GUIDE.md:100:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast while
./GUIDE.md:101:119:### Is it really faster than everything else?
./GUIDE.md:102:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast because:
./GUIDE.md:103:129:  optimizations to make searching very fast.
./GUIDE.md:104:```
./GUIDE.md:105:
./GUIDE.md:106:In this case, we used `fast\w*` for our pattern instead of `fast\w+`. The `*`
./GUIDE.md:107:means that it should match *zero* or more times. In this case, ripgrep will
./GUIDE.md:108:print the same lines as the pattern `fast`, but if your terminal supports
./GUIDE.md:109:colors, you'll notice that `faster` will be highlighted instead of just the
./GUIDE.md:110:`fast` prefix.
./GUIDE.md:111:
./GUIDE.md:112:It is beyond the scope of this guide to provide a full tutorial on regular
./GUIDE.md:113:expressions, but ripgrep's specific syntax is documented here:
./GUIDE.md:114:https://docs.rs/regex/*/regex/#syntax
./GUIDE.md:115:
./GUIDE.md:116:
./GUIDE.md:117:### Recursive search
./GUIDE.md:118:
./GUIDE.md:119:In the previous section, we showed how to use ripgrep to search a single file.
./GUIDE.md:120:In this section, we'll show how to use ripgrep to search an entire directory
./GUIDE.md:121:of files. In fact, *recursively* searching your current working directory is
./GUIDE.md:122:the default mode of operation for ripgrep, which means doing this is very
./GUIDE.md:123:simple.
./GUIDE.md:124:
./GUIDE.md:125:Using our unzipped archive of ripgrep source code, here's how to find all
./GUIDE.md:126:function definitions whose name is `write`:
./GUIDE.md:127:
./GUIDE.md:128:```
./GUIDE.md:129:$ rg 'fn write\('
./GUIDE.md:130:src/printer.rs
./GUIDE.md:131:469:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) {
./GUIDE.md:132:
./GUIDE.md:133:termcolor/src/lib.rs
./GUIDE.md:134:227:    fn write(&mut self, b: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:135:250:    fn write(&mut self, b: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:136:428:    fn write(&mut self, b: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> { self.wtr.write(b) }
./GUIDE.md:137:441:    fn write(&mut self, b: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> { self.wtr.write(b) }
./GUIDE.md:138:454:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:139:511:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:140:848:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:141:915:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:142:949:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:143:1114:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:144:1348:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:145:1353:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
./GUIDE.md:146:```
./GUIDE.md:147:
./GUIDE.md:148:(**Note:** We escape the `(` here because `(` has special significance inside
./GUIDE.md:149:regular expressions. You could also use `rg -F 'fn write('` to achieve the
./GUIDE.md:150:same thing, where `-F` interprets your pattern as a literal string instead of
./GUIDE.md:151:a regular expression.)
./GUIDE.md:152:
./GUIDE.md:153:In this example, we didn't specify a file at all. Instead, ripgrep defaulted
./GUIDE.md:154:to searching your current directory in the absence of a path. In general,
./GUIDE.md:155:`rg foo` is equivalent to `rg foo ./`.
./GUIDE.md:156:
./GUIDE.md:157:This particular search showed us results in both the `src` and `termcolor`
./GUIDE.md:158:directories. The `src` directory is the core ripgrep code where as `termcolor`
./GUIDE.md:159:is a dependency of ripgrep (and is used by other tools). What if we only wanted
./GUIDE.md:160:to search core ripgrep code? Well, that's easy, just specify the directory you
./GUIDE.md:161:want:
./GUIDE.md:162:
./GUIDE.md:163:```
./GUIDE.md:164:$ rg 'fn write\(' src
./GUIDE.md:165:src/printer.rs
./GUIDE.md:166:469:    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) {
./GUIDE.md:167:```
./GUIDE.md:168:
./GUIDE.md:169:Here, ripgrep limited its search to the `src` directory. Another way of doing
./GUIDE.md:170:this search would be to `cd` into the `src` directory and simply use `rg 'fn
./GUIDE.md:171:write\('` again.
./GUIDE.md:172:
./GUIDE.md:173:
./GUIDE.md:174:### Automatic filtering
./GUIDE.md:175:
./GUIDE.md:176:After recursive search, ripgrep's most important feature is what it *doesn't*
./GUIDE.md:177:search. By default, when you search a directory, ripgrep will ignore all of
./GUIDE.md:178:the following:
./GUIDE.md:179:
./GUIDE.md:180:1. Files and directories that match glob patterns in these three categories:
./GUIDE.md:181:      1. `.gitignore` globs (including global and repo-specific globs). This
./GUIDE.md:182:         includes `.gitignore` files in parent directories that are part of the
./GUIDE.md:183:         same `git` repository. (Unless the `--no-require-git` flag is given.)
./GUIDE.md:184:      2. `.ignore` globs, which take precedence over all gitignore globs
./GUIDE.md:185:         when there's a conflict. This includes `.ignore` files in parent
./GUIDE.md:186:         directories.
./GUIDE.md:187:      3. `.rgignore` globs, which take precedence over all `.ignore` globs
./GUIDE.md:188:         when there's a conflict. This includes `.rgignore` files in parent
./GUIDE.md:189:         directories.
./GUIDE.md:190:2. Hidden files and directories.
./GUIDE.md:191:3. Binary files. (ripgrep considers any file with a `NUL` byte to be binary.)
./GUIDE.md:192:4. Symbolic links aren't followed.
./GUIDE.md:193:
./GUIDE.md:194:All of these things can be toggled using various flags provided by ripgrep:
./GUIDE.md:195:
./GUIDE.md:196:1. You can disable all ignore-related filtering with the `--no-ignore` flag.
./GUIDE.md:197:2. Hidden files and directories can be searched with the `--hidden` (`-.` for
./GUIDE.md:198:short) flag.
./GUIDE.md:199:3. Binary files can be searched via the `--text` (`-a` for short) flag.
./GUIDE.md:200:   Be careful with this flag! Binary files may emit control characters to your
./GUIDE.md:201:   terminal, which might cause strange behavior.
./GUIDE.md:202:4. ripgrep can follow symlinks with the `--follow` (`-L` for short) flag.
./GUIDE.md:203:
./GUIDE.md:204:As a special convenience, ripgrep also provides a flag called `--unrestricted`
./GUIDE.md:205:(`-u` for short). Repeated uses of this flag will cause ripgrep to disable
./GUIDE.md:206:more and more of its filtering. That is, `-u` will disable `.gitignore`
./GUIDE.md:207:handling, `-uu` will search hidden files and directories and `-uuu` will search
./GUIDE.md:208:binary files. This is useful when you're using ripgrep and you aren't sure
./GUIDE.md:209:whether its filtering is hiding results from you. Tacking on a couple `-u`
./GUIDE.md:210:flags is a quick way to find out. (Use the `--debug` flag if you're still
./GUIDE.md:211:perplexed, and if that doesn't help,
./GUIDE.md:212:[file an issue](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/new).)
./GUIDE.md:213:
./GUIDE.md:214:ripgrep's `.gitignore` handling actually goes a bit beyond just `.gitignore`
./GUIDE.md:215:files. ripgrep will also respect repository specific rules found in
./GUIDE.md:216:`$GIT_DIR/info/exclude`, as well as any global ignore rules in your
./GUIDE.md:217:`core.excludesFile` (which is usually `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore` on
./GUIDE.md:218:Unix-like systems).
./GUIDE.md:219:
./GUIDE.md:220:Sometimes you want to search files that are in your `.gitignore`, so it is
./GUIDE.md:221:possible to specify additional ignore rules or overrides in a `.ignore`
./GUIDE.md:222:(application agnostic) or `.rgignore` (ripgrep specific) file.
./GUIDE.md:223:
./GUIDE.md:224:For example, let's say you have a `.gitignore` file that looks like this:
./GUIDE.md:225:
./GUIDE.md:226:```
./GUIDE.md:227:log/
./GUIDE.md:228:```
./GUIDE.md:229:
./GUIDE.md:230:This generally means that any `log` directory won't be tracked by `git`.
./GUIDE.md:231:However, perhaps it contains useful output that you'd like to include in your
./GUIDE.md:232:searches, but you still don't want to track it in `git`. You can achieve this
./GUIDE.md:233:by creating a `.ignore` file in the same directory as the `.gitignore` file
./GUIDE.md:234:with the following contents:
./GUIDE.md:235:
./GUIDE.md:236:```
./GUIDE.md:237:!log/
./GUIDE.md:238:```
./GUIDE.md:239:
./GUIDE.md:240:ripgrep treats `.ignore` files with higher precedence than `.gitignore` files
./GUIDE.md:241:(and treats `.rgignore` files with higher precedence than `.ignore` files).
./GUIDE.md:242:This means ripgrep will see the `!log/` whitelist rule first and search that
./GUIDE.md:243:directory.
./GUIDE.md:244:
./GUIDE.md:245:Like `.gitignore`, a `.ignore` file can be placed in any directory. Its rules
./GUIDE.md:246:will be processed with respect to the directory it resides in, just like
./GUIDE.md:247:`.gitignore`.
./GUIDE.md:248:
./GUIDE.md:249:To process `.gitignore` and `.ignore` files case insensitively, use the flag
./GUIDE.md:250:`--ignore-file-case-insensitive`. This is especially useful on case insensitive
./GUIDE.md:251:file systems like those on Windows and macOS. Note though that this can come
./GUIDE.md:252:with a significant performance penalty, and is therefore disabled by default.
./GUIDE.md:253:
./GUIDE.md:254:For a more in depth description of how glob patterns in a `.gitignore` file
./GUIDE.md:255:are interpreted, please see `man gitignore`.
./GUIDE.md:256:
./GUIDE.md:257:
./GUIDE.md:258:### Manual filtering: globs
./GUIDE.md:259:
./GUIDE.md:260:In the previous section, we talked about ripgrep's filtering that it does by
./GUIDE.md:261:default. It is "automatic" because it reacts to your environment. That is, it
./GUIDE.md:262:uses already existing `.gitignore` files to produce more relevant search
./GUIDE.md:263:results.
./GUIDE.md:264:
./GUIDE.md:265:In addition to automatic filtering, ripgrep also provides more manual or ad hoc
./GUIDE.md:266:filtering. This comes in two varieties: additional glob patterns specified in
./GUIDE.md:267:your ripgrep commands and file type filtering. This section covers glob
./GUIDE.md:268:patterns while the next section covers file type filtering.
./GUIDE.md:269:
./GUIDE.md:270:In our ripgrep source code (see [Basics](#basics) for instructions on how to
./GUIDE.md:271:get a source archive to search), let's say we wanted to see which things depend
./GUIDE.md:272:on `lexopt`, our argument parser.
./GUIDE.md:273:
./GUIDE.md:274:We could do this:
./GUIDE.md:275:
./GUIDE.md:276:```
./GUIDE.md:277:$ rg lexopt
./GUIDE.md:278:[lots of results]
./GUIDE.md:279:```
./GUIDE.md:280:
./GUIDE.md:281:But this shows us many things, and we're only interested in where we wrote
./GUIDE.md:282:`lexopt` as a dependency. Instead, we could limit ourselves to TOML files,
./GUIDE.md:283:which is how dependencies are communicated to Rust's build tool, Cargo:
./GUIDE.md:284:
./GUIDE.md:285:```
./GUIDE.md:286:$ rg lexopt -g '*.toml'
./GUIDE.md:287:Cargo.toml
./GUIDE.md:288:57:lexopt = "0.3.0"
./GUIDE.md:289:```
./GUIDE.md:290:
./GUIDE.md:291:The `-g '*.toml'` syntax says, "make sure every file searched matches this
./GUIDE.md:292:glob pattern." Note that we put `'*.toml'` in single quotes to prevent our
./GUIDE.md:293:shell from expanding the `*`.
./GUIDE.md:294:
./GUIDE.md:295:If we wanted, we could tell ripgrep to search anything *but* `*.toml` files:
./GUIDE.md:296:
./GUIDE.md:297:```
./GUIDE.md:298:$ rg lexopt -g '!*.toml'
./GUIDE.md:299:[lots of results]
./GUIDE.md:300:```
./GUIDE.md:301:
./GUIDE.md:302:This will give you a lot of results again as above, but they won't include
./GUIDE.md:303:files ending with `.toml`. Note that the use of a `!` here to mean "negation"
./GUIDE.md:304:is a bit non-standard, but it was chosen to be consistent with how globs in
./GUIDE.md:305:`.gitignore` files are written. (Although, the meaning is reversed. In
./GUIDE.md:306:`.gitignore` files, a `!` prefix means whitelist, and on the command line, a
./GUIDE.md:307:`!` means blacklist.)
./GUIDE.md:308:
./GUIDE.md:309:Globs are interpreted in exactly the same way as `.gitignore` patterns. That
./GUIDE.md:310:is, later globs will override earlier globs. For example, the following command
./GUIDE.md:311:will search only `*.toml` files:
./GUIDE.md:312:
./GUIDE.md:313:```
./GUIDE.md:314:$ rg lexopt -g '!*.toml' -g '*.toml'
./GUIDE.md:315:```
./GUIDE.md:316:
./GUIDE.md:317:Interestingly, reversing the order of the globs in this case will match
./GUIDE.md:318:nothing, since the presence of at least one non-blacklist glob will institute a
./GUIDE.md:319:requirement that every file searched must match at least one glob. In this
./GUIDE.md:320:case, the blacklist glob takes precedence over the previous glob and prevents
./GUIDE.md:321:any file from being searched at all!
./GUIDE.md:322:
./GUIDE.md:323:
./GUIDE.md:324:### Manual filtering: file types
./GUIDE.md:325:
./GUIDE.md:326:Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
./GUIDE.md:327:For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
./GUIDE.md:328:want to see results for Rust files:
./GUIDE.md:329:
./GUIDE.md:330:```
./GUIDE.md:331:$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
./GUIDE.md:332:```
./GUIDE.md:333:
./GUIDE.md:334:Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
./GUIDE.md:335:file types:
./GUIDE.md:336:
./GUIDE.md:337:```
./GUIDE.md:338:$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
./GUIDE.md:339:```
./GUIDE.md:340:
./GUIDE.md:341:or, more succinctly,
./GUIDE.md:342:
./GUIDE.md:343:```
./GUIDE.md:344:$ rg 'fn run' -trust
./GUIDE.md:345:```
./GUIDE.md:346:
./GUIDE.md:347:The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
./GUIDE.md:348:assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
./GUIDE.md:349:write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
./GUIDE.md:350:example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
./GUIDE.md:351:files and C header files:
./GUIDE.md:352:
./GUIDE.md:353:```
./GUIDE.md:354:$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
./GUIDE.md:355:```
./GUIDE.md:356:
./GUIDE.md:357:or you could just use the C file type:
./GUIDE.md:358:
./GUIDE.md:359:```
./GUIDE.md:360:$ rg 'int main' -tc
./GUIDE.md:361:```
./GUIDE.md:362:
./GUIDE.md:363:Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:
./GUIDE.md:364:
./GUIDE.md:365:```
./GUIDE.md:366:$ rg lexopt --type-not rust
./GUIDE.md:367:```
./GUIDE.md:368:
./GUIDE.md:369:or, more succinctly,
./GUIDE.md:370:
./GUIDE.md:371:```
./GUIDE.md:372:$ rg lexopt -Trust
./GUIDE.md:373:```
./GUIDE.md:374:
./GUIDE.md:375:That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
./GUIDE.md:376:files of this type."
./GUIDE.md:377:
./GUIDE.md:378:To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:
./GUIDE.md:379:
./GUIDE.md:380:```
./GUIDE.md:381:$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
./GUIDE.md:382:make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
./GUIDE.md:383:```
./GUIDE.md:384:
./GUIDE.md:385:By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
./GUIDE.md:386:types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
./GUIDE.md:387:types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
./GUIDE.md:388:consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:
./GUIDE.md:389:
./GUIDE.md:390:```
./GUIDE.md:391:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
./GUIDE.md:392:```
./GUIDE.md:393:
./GUIDE.md:394:or, more succinctly,
./GUIDE.md:395:
./GUIDE.md:396:```
./GUIDE.md:397:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
./GUIDE.md:398:```
./GUIDE.md:399:
./GUIDE.md:400:The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
./GUIDE.md:401:`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
./GUIDE.md:402:the pattern `title`. If you ran
./GUIDE.md:403:
./GUIDE.md:404:```
./GUIDE.md:405:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
./GUIDE.md:406:```
./GUIDE.md:407:
./GUIDE.md:408:Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
./GUIDE.md:409:part of ripgrep's built-in types.
./GUIDE.md:410:
./GUIDE.md:411:It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
./GUIDE.md:412:current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
./GUIDE.md:413:persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
./GUIDE.md:414:then you should either create a shell alias:
./GUIDE.md:415:
./GUIDE.md:416:```
./GUIDE.md:417:alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
./GUIDE.md:418:```
./GUIDE.md:419:
./GUIDE.md:420:or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
./GUIDE.md:421:([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)
./GUIDE.md:422:
./GUIDE.md:423:#### The special `all` file type
./GUIDE.md:424:
./GUIDE.md:425:A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
./GUIDE.md:426:for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
./GUIDE.md:427:including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
./GUIDE.md:428:to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
./GUIDE.md:429:stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.
./GUIDE.md:430:
./GUIDE.md:431:As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
./GUIDE.md:432:`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
./GUIDE.md:433:Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
./GUIDE.md:434:`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
./GUIDE.md:435:by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
./GUIDE.md:436:other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
./GUIDE.md:437:`my-shell-library.bash`.
./GUIDE.md:438:
./GUIDE.md:439:### Replacements
./GUIDE.md:440:
./GUIDE.md:441:ripgrep provides a limited ability to modify its output by replacing matched
./GUIDE.md:442:text with some other text. This is easiest to explain with an example. Remember
./GUIDE.md:443:when we searched for the word `fast` in ripgrep's README?
./GUIDE.md:444:
./GUIDE.md:445:```
./GUIDE.md:446:$ rg fast README.md
./GUIDE.md:447:75:  faster than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement
./GUIDE.md:448:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast while
./GUIDE.md:449:119:### Is it really faster than everything else?
./GUIDE.md:450:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast because:
./GUIDE.md:451:129:  optimizations to make searching very fast.
./GUIDE.md:452:```
./GUIDE.md:453:
./GUIDE.md:454:What if we wanted to *replace* all occurrences of `fast` with `FAST`? That's
./GUIDE.md:455:easy with ripgrep's `--replace` flag:
./GUIDE.md:456:
./GUIDE.md:457:```
./GUIDE.md:458:$ rg fast README.md --replace FAST
./GUIDE.md:459:75:  FASTer than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement
./GUIDE.md:460:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays FAST while
./GUIDE.md:461:119:### Is it really FASTer than everything else?
./GUIDE.md:462:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is FAST because:
./GUIDE.md:463:129:  optimizations to make searching very FAST.
./GUIDE.md:464:```
./GUIDE.md:465:
./GUIDE.md:466:or, more succinctly,
./GUIDE.md:467:
./GUIDE.md:468:```
./GUIDE.md:469:$ rg fast README.md -r FAST
./GUIDE.md:470:[snip]
./GUIDE.md:471:```
./GUIDE.md:472:
./GUIDE.md:473:In essence, the `--replace` flag applies *only* to the matching portion of text
./GUIDE.md:474:in the output. If you instead wanted to replace an entire line of text, then
./GUIDE.md:475:you need to include the entire line in your match. For example:
./GUIDE.md:476:
./GUIDE.md:477:```
./GUIDE.md:478:$ rg '^.*fast.*$' README.md -r FAST
./GUIDE.md:479:75:FAST
./GUIDE.md:480:88:FAST
./GUIDE.md:481:119:FAST
./GUIDE.md:482:124:FAST
./GUIDE.md:483:129:FAST
./GUIDE.md:484:```
./GUIDE.md:485:
./GUIDE.md:486:Alternatively, you can combine the `--only-matching` (or `-o` for short) with
./GUIDE.md:487:the `--replace` flag to achieve the same result:
./GUIDE.md:488:
./GUIDE.md:489:```
./GUIDE.md:490:$ rg fast README.md --only-matching --replace FAST
./GUIDE.md:491:75:FAST
./GUIDE.md:492:88:FAST
./GUIDE.md:493:119:FAST
./GUIDE.md:494:124:FAST
./GUIDE.md:495:129:FAST
./GUIDE.md:496:```
./GUIDE.md:497:
./GUIDE.md:498:or, more succinctly,
./GUIDE.md:499:
./GUIDE.md:500:```
./GUIDE.md:501:$ rg fast README.md -or FAST
./GUIDE.md:502:[snip]
./GUIDE.md:503:```
./GUIDE.md:504:
./GUIDE.md:505:Finally, replacements can include capturing groups. For example, let's say
./GUIDE.md:506:we wanted to find all occurrences of `fast` followed by another word and
./GUIDE.md:507:join them together with a dash. The pattern we might use for that is
./GUIDE.md:508:`fast\s+(\w+)`, which matches `fast`, followed by any amount of whitespace,
./GUIDE.md:509:followed by any number of "word" characters. We put the `\w+` in a "capturing
./GUIDE.md:510:group" (indicated by parentheses) so that we can reference it later in our
./GUIDE.md:511:replacement string. For example:
./GUIDE.md:512:
./GUIDE.md:513:```
./GUIDE.md:514:$ rg 'fast\s+(\w+)' README.md -r 'fast-$1'
./GUIDE.md:515:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast-while
./GUIDE.md:516:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast-because:
./GUIDE.md:517:```
./GUIDE.md:518:
./GUIDE.md:519:Our replacement string here, `fast-$1`, consists of `fast-` followed by the
./GUIDE.md:520:contents of the capturing group at index `1`. (Capturing groups actually start
./GUIDE.md:521:at index 0, but the `0`th capturing group always corresponds to the entire
./GUIDE.md:522:match. The capturing group at index `1` always corresponds to the first
./GUIDE.md:523:explicit capturing group found in the regex pattern.)
./GUIDE.md:524:
./GUIDE.md:525:Capturing groups can also be named, which is sometimes more convenient than
./GUIDE.md:526:using the indices. For example, the following command is equivalent to the
./GUIDE.md:527:above command:
./GUIDE.md:528:
./GUIDE.md:529:```
./GUIDE.md:530:$ rg 'fast\s+(?P<word>\w+)' README.md -r 'fast-$word'
./GUIDE.md:531:88:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast-while
./GUIDE.md:532:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast-because:
./GUIDE.md:533:```
./GUIDE.md:534:
./GUIDE.md:535:It is important to note that ripgrep **will never modify your files**. The
./GUIDE.md:536:`--replace` flag only controls ripgrep's output. (And there is no flag to let
./GUIDE.md:537:you do a replacement in a file.)
./GUIDE.md:538:
./GUIDE.md:539:
./GUIDE.md:540:### Configuration file
./GUIDE.md:541:
./GUIDE.md:542:It is possible that ripgrep's default options aren't suitable in every case.
./GUIDE.md:543:For that reason, and because shell aliases aren't always convenient, ripgrep
./GUIDE.md:544:supports configuration files.
./GUIDE.md:545:
./GUIDE.md:546:Setting up a configuration file is simple. ripgrep will not look in any
./GUIDE.md:547:predetermined directory for a config file automatically. Instead, you need to
./GUIDE.md:548:set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to the file path of your
./GUIDE.md:549:config file. Once the environment variable is set, open the file and just type
./GUIDE.md:550:in the flags you want set automatically. There are only two rules for
./GUIDE.md:551:describing the format of the config file:
./GUIDE.md:552:
./GUIDE.md:553:1. Every line is a shell argument, after trimming whitespace.
./GUIDE.md:554:2. Lines starting with `#` (optionally preceded by any amount of whitespace)
./GUIDE.md:555:are ignored.
./GUIDE.md:556:
./GUIDE.md:557:In particular, there is no escaping. Each line is given to ripgrep as a single
./GUIDE.md:558:command line argument verbatim.
./GUIDE.md:559:
./GUIDE.md:560:Here's an example of a configuration file, which demonstrates some of the
./GUIDE.md:561:formatting peculiarities:
./GUIDE.md:562:
./GUIDE.md:563:```
./GUIDE.md:564:$ cat $HOME/.ripgreprc
./GUIDE.md:565:# Don't let ripgrep vomit really long lines to my terminal, and show a preview.
./GUIDE.md:566:--max-columns=150
./GUIDE.md:567:--max-columns-preview
./GUIDE.md:568:
./GUIDE.md:569:# Add my 'web' type.
./GUIDE.md:570:--type-add
./GUIDE.md:571:web:*.{html,css,js}*
./GUIDE.md:572:
./GUIDE.md:573:# Search hidden files / directories (e.g. dotfiles) by default
./GUIDE.md:574:--hidden
./GUIDE.md:575:
./GUIDE.md:576:# Using glob patterns to include/exclude files or folders
./GUIDE.md:577:--glob=!.git/*
./GUIDE.md:578:
./GUIDE.md:579:# or
./GUIDE.md:580:--glob
./GUIDE.md:581:!.git/*
./GUIDE.md:582:
./GUIDE.md:583:# Set the colors.
./GUIDE.md:584:--colors=line:none
./GUIDE.md:585:--colors=line:style:bold
./GUIDE.md:586:
./GUIDE.md:587:# Because who cares about case!?
./GUIDE.md:588:--smart-case
./GUIDE.md:589:```
./GUIDE.md:590:
./GUIDE.md:591:When we use a flag that has a value, we either put the flag and the value on
./GUIDE.md:592:the same line but delimited by an `=` sign (e.g., `--max-columns=150`), or we
./GUIDE.md:593:put the flag and the value on two different lines. This is because ripgrep's
./GUIDE.md:594:argument parser knows to treat the single argument `--max-columns=150` as a
./GUIDE.md:595:flag with a value, but if we had written `--max-columns 150` in our
./GUIDE.md:596:configuration file, then ripgrep's argument parser wouldn't know what to do
./GUIDE.md:597:with it.
./GUIDE.md:598:
./GUIDE.md:599:Putting the flag and value on different lines is exactly equivalent and is a
./GUIDE.md:600:matter of style.
./GUIDE.md:601:
./GUIDE.md:602:Comments are encouraged so that you remember what the config is doing. Empty
./GUIDE.md:603:lines are OK too.
./GUIDE.md:604:
./GUIDE.md:605:So let's say you're using the above configuration file, but while you're at a
./GUIDE.md:606:terminal, you really want to be able to see lines longer than 150 columns. What
./GUIDE.md:607:do you do? Thankfully, all you need to do is pass `--max-columns 0` (or `-M0`
./GUIDE.md:608:for short) on the command line, which will override your configuration file's
./GUIDE.md:609:setting. This works because ripgrep's configuration file is *prepended* to the
./GUIDE.md:610:explicit arguments you give it on the command line. Since flags given later
./GUIDE.md:611:override flags given earlier, everything works as expected. This works for most
./GUIDE.md:612:other flags as well, and each flag's documentation states which other flags
./GUIDE.md:613:override it.
./GUIDE.md:614:
./GUIDE.md:615:If you're confused about what configuration file ripgrep is reading arguments
./GUIDE.md:616:from, then running ripgrep with the `--debug` flag should help clarify things.
./GUIDE.md:617:The debug output should note what config file is being loaded and the arguments
./GUIDE.md:618:that have been read from the configuration.
./GUIDE.md:619:
./GUIDE.md:620:Finally, if you want to make absolutely sure that ripgrep *isn't* reading a
./GUIDE.md:621:configuration file, then you can pass the `--no-config` flag, which will always
./GUIDE.md:622:prevent ripgrep from reading extraneous configuration from the environment,
./GUIDE.md:623:regardless of what other methods of configuration are added to ripgrep in the
./GUIDE.md:624:future.
./GUIDE.md:625:
./GUIDE.md:626:
./GUIDE.md:627:### File encoding
./GUIDE.md:628:
./GUIDE.md:629:[Text encoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encoding) is a complex
./GUIDE.md:630:topic, but we can try to summarize its relevancy to ripgrep:
./GUIDE.md:631:
./GUIDE.md:632:* Files are generally just a bundle of bytes. There is no reliable way to know
./GUIDE.md:633:  their encoding.
./GUIDE.md:634:* Either the encoding of the pattern must match the encoding of the files being
./GUIDE.md:635:  searched, or a form of transcoding must be performed that converts either the
./GUIDE.md:636:  pattern or the file to the same encoding as the other.
./GUIDE.md:637:* ripgrep tends to work best on plain text files, and among plain text files,
./GUIDE.md:638:  the most popular encodings likely consist of ASCII, latin1 or UTF-8. As
./GUIDE.md:639:  a special exception, UTF-16 is prevalent in Windows environments
./GUIDE.md:640:
./GUIDE.md:641:In light of the above, here is how ripgrep behaves when `--encoding auto` is
./GUIDE.md:642:given, which is the default:
./GUIDE.md:643:
./GUIDE.md:644:* All input is assumed to be ASCII compatible (which means every byte that
./GUIDE.md:645:  corresponds to an ASCII codepoint actually is an ASCII codepoint). This
./GUIDE.md:646:  includes ASCII itself, latin1 and UTF-8.
./GUIDE.md:647:* ripgrep works best with UTF-8. For example, ripgrep's regular expression
./GUIDE.md:648:  engine supports Unicode features. Namely, character classes like `\w` will
./GUIDE.md:649:  match all word characters by Unicode's definition and `.` will match any
./GUIDE.md:650:  Unicode codepoint instead of any byte. These constructions assume UTF-8,
./GUIDE.md:651:  so they simply won't match when they come across bytes in a file that aren't
./GUIDE.md:652:  UTF-8.
./GUIDE.md:653:* To handle the UTF-16 case, ripgrep will do something called "BOM sniffing"
./GUIDE.md:654:  by default. That is, the first three bytes of a file will be read, and if
./GUIDE.md:655:  they correspond to a UTF-16 BOM, then ripgrep will transcode the contents of
./GUIDE.md:656:  the file from UTF-16 to UTF-8, and then execute the search on the transcoded
./GUIDE.md:657:  version of the file. (This incurs a performance penalty since transcoding
./GUIDE.md:658:  is needed in addition to regex searching.) If the file contains invalid
./GUIDE.md:659:  UTF-16, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is substituted in place of
./GUIDE.md:660:  invalid code units.
./GUIDE.md:661:* To handle other cases, ripgrep provides a `-E/--encoding` flag, which permits
./GUIDE.md:662:  you to specify an encoding from the
./GUIDE.md:663:  [Encoding Standard](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-encoding-get).
./GUIDE.md:664:  ripgrep will assume *all* files searched are the encoding specified (unless
./GUIDE.md:665:  the file has a BOM) and will perform a transcoding step just like in the
./GUIDE.md:666:  UTF-16 case described above.
./GUIDE.md:667:
./GUIDE.md:668:By default, ripgrep will not require its input be valid UTF-8. That is, ripgrep
./GUIDE.md:669:can and will search arbitrary bytes. The key here is that if you're searching
./GUIDE.md:670:content that isn't UTF-8, then the usefulness of your pattern will degrade. If
./GUIDE.md:671:you're searching bytes that aren't ASCII compatible, then it's likely the
./GUIDE.md:672:pattern won't find anything. With all that said, this mode of operation is
./GUIDE.md:673:important, because it lets you find ASCII or UTF-8 *within* files that are
./GUIDE.md:674:otherwise arbitrary bytes.
./GUIDE.md:675:
./GUIDE.md:676:As a special case, the `-E/--encoding` flag supports the value `none`, which
./GUIDE.md:677:will completely disable all encoding related logic, including BOM sniffing.
./GUIDE.md:678:When `-E/--encoding` is set to `none`, ripgrep will search the raw bytes of
./GUIDE.md:679:the underlying file with no transcoding step. For example, here's how you might
./GUIDE.md:680:search the raw UTF-16 encoding of the string `Шерлок`:
./GUIDE.md:681:
./GUIDE.md:682:```
./GUIDE.md:683:$ rg '(?-u)\(\x045\x04@\x04;\x04>\x04:\x04' -E none -a some-utf16-file
./GUIDE.md:684:```
./GUIDE.md:685:
./GUIDE.md:686:Of course, that's just an example meant to show how one can drop down into
./GUIDE.md:687:raw bytes. Namely, the simpler command works as you might expect automatically:
./GUIDE.md:688:
./GUIDE.md:689:```
./GUIDE.md:690:$ rg 'Шерлок' some-utf16-file
./GUIDE.md:691:```
./GUIDE.md:692:
./GUIDE.md:693:Finally, it is possible to disable ripgrep's Unicode support from within the
./GUIDE.md:694:regular expression. For example, let's say you wanted `.` to match any byte
./GUIDE.md:695:rather than any Unicode codepoint. (You might want this while searching a
./GUIDE.md:696:binary file, since `.` by default will not match invalid UTF-8.) You could do
./GUIDE.md:697:this by disabling Unicode via a regular expression flag:
./GUIDE.md:698:
./GUIDE.md:699:```
./GUIDE.md:700:$ rg '(?-u:.)'
./GUIDE.md:701:```
./GUIDE.md:702:
./GUIDE.md:703:This works for any part of the pattern. For example, the following will find
./GUIDE.md:704:any Unicode word character followed by any ASCII word character followed by
./GUIDE.md:705:another Unicode word character:
./GUIDE.md:706:
./GUIDE.md:707:```
./GUIDE.md:708:$ rg '\w(?-u:\w)\w'
./GUIDE.md:709:```
./GUIDE.md:710:
./GUIDE.md:711:
./GUIDE.md:712:### Binary data
./GUIDE.md:713:
./GUIDE.md:714:In addition to skipping hidden files and files in your `.gitignore` by default,
./GUIDE.md:715:ripgrep also attempts to skip binary files. ripgrep does this by default
./GUIDE.md:716:because binary files (like PDFs or images) are typically not things you want to
./GUIDE.md:717:search when searching for regex matches. Moreover, if content in a binary file
./GUIDE.md:718:did match, then it's possible for undesirable binary data to be printed to your
./GUIDE.md:719:terminal and wreak havoc.
./GUIDE.md:720:
./GUIDE.md:721:Unfortunately, unlike skipping hidden files and respecting your `.gitignore`
./GUIDE.md:722:rules, a file cannot as easily be classified as binary. In order to figure out
./GUIDE.md:723:whether a file is binary, the most effective heuristic that balances
./GUIDE.md:724:correctness with performance is to simply look for `NUL` bytes. At that point,
./GUIDE.md:725:the determination is simple: a file is considered "binary" if and only if it
./GUIDE.md:726:contains a `NUL` byte somewhere in its contents.
./GUIDE.md:727:
./GUIDE.md:728:The issue is that while most binary files will have a `NUL` byte toward the
./GUIDE.md:729:beginning of its contents, this is not necessarily true. The `NUL` byte might
./GUIDE.md:730:be the very last byte in a large file, but that file is still considered
./GUIDE.md:731:binary. While this leads to a fair amount of complexity inside ripgrep's
./GUIDE.md:732:implementation, it also results in some unintuitive user experiences.
./GUIDE.md:733:
./GUIDE.md:734:At a high level, ripgrep operates in three different modes with respect to
./GUIDE.md:735:binary files:
./GUIDE.md:736:
./GUIDE.md:737:1. The default mode is to attempt to remove binary files from a search
./GUIDE.md:738:   completely. This is meant to mirror how ripgrep removes hidden files and
./GUIDE.md:739:   files in your `.gitignore` automatically. That is, as soon as a file is
./GUIDE.md:740:   detected as binary, searching stops. If a match was already printed (because
./GUIDE.md:741:   it was detected long before a `NUL` byte), then ripgrep will print a warning
./GUIDE.md:742:   message indicating that the search stopped prematurely. This default mode
./GUIDE.md:743:   **only applies to files searched by ripgrep as a result of recursive
./GUIDE.md:744:   directory traversal**, which is consistent with ripgrep's other automatic
./GUIDE.md:745:   filtering. For example, `rg foo .file` will search `.file` even though it
./GUIDE.md:746:   is hidden. Similarly, `rg foo binary-file` will search `binary-file` in
./GUIDE.md:747:   "binary" mode automatically.
./GUIDE.md:748:2. Binary mode is similar to the default mode, except it will not always
./GUIDE.md:749:   stop searching after it sees a `NUL` byte. Namely, in this mode, ripgrep
./GUIDE.md:750:   will continue searching a file that is known to be binary until the first
./GUIDE.md:751:   of two conditions is met: 1) the end of the file has been reached or 2) a
./GUIDE.md:752:   match is or has been seen. This means that in binary mode, if ripgrep
./GUIDE.md:753:   reports no matches, then there are no matches in the file. When a match does
./GUIDE.md:754:   occur, ripgrep prints a message similar to one it prints when in its default
./GUIDE.md:755:   mode indicating that the search has stopped prematurely. This mode can be
./GUIDE.md:756:   forcefully enabled for all files with the `--binary` flag. The purpose of
./GUIDE.md:757:   binary mode is to provide a way to discover matches in all files, but to
./GUIDE.md:758:   avoid having binary data dumped into your terminal.
./GUIDE.md:759:3. Text mode completely disables all binary detection and searches all files
./GUIDE.md:760:   as if they were text. This is useful when searching a file that is
./GUIDE.md:761:   predominantly text but contains a `NUL` byte, or if you are specifically
./GUIDE.md:762:   trying to search binary data. This mode can be enabled with the `-a/--text`
./GUIDE.md:763:   flag. Note that when using this mode on very large binary files, it is
./GUIDE.md:764:   possible for ripgrep to use a lot of memory.
./GUIDE.md:765:
./GUIDE.md:766:Unfortunately, there is one additional complexity in ripgrep that can make it
./GUIDE.md:767:difficult to reason about binary files. That is, the way binary detection works
./GUIDE.md:768:depends on the way that ripgrep searches your files. Specifically:
./GUIDE.md:769:
./GUIDE.md:770:* When ripgrep uses memory maps, then binary detection is only performed on the
./GUIDE.md:771:  first few kilobytes of the file in addition to every matching line.
./GUIDE.md:772:* When ripgrep doesn't use memory maps, then binary detection is performed on
./GUIDE.md:773:  all bytes searched.
./GUIDE.md:774:
./GUIDE.md:775:This means that whether a file is detected as binary or not can change based
./GUIDE.md:776:on the internal search strategy used by ripgrep. If you prefer to keep
./GUIDE.md:777:ripgrep's binary file detection consistent, then you can disable memory maps
./GUIDE.md:778:via the `--no-mmap` flag. (The cost will be a small performance regression when
./GUIDE.md:779:searching very large files on some platforms.)
./GUIDE.md:780:
./GUIDE.md:781:
./GUIDE.md:782:### Preprocessor
./GUIDE.md:783:
./GUIDE.md:784:In ripgrep, a preprocessor is any type of command that can be run to transform
./GUIDE.md:785:the input of every file before ripgrep searches it. This makes it possible to
./GUIDE.md:786:search virtually any kind of content that can be automatically converted to
./GUIDE.md:787:text without having to teach ripgrep how to read said content.
./GUIDE.md:788:
./GUIDE.md:789:One common example is searching PDFs. PDFs are first and foremost meant to be
./GUIDE.md:790:displayed to users. But PDFs often have text streams in them that can be useful
./GUIDE.md:791:to search. In our case, we want to search Bruce Watson's excellent
./GUIDE.md:792:dissertation,
./GUIDE.md:793:[Taxonomies and Toolkits of Regular Language Algorithms](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/1995-watson.pdf).
./GUIDE.md:794:After downloading it, let's try searching it:
./GUIDE.md:795:
./GUIDE.md:796:```
./GUIDE.md:797:$ rg 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf
./GUIDE.md:798:$
./GUIDE.md:799:```
./GUIDE.md:800:
./GUIDE.md:801:Surely, a dissertation on regular language algorithms would mention
./GUIDE.md:802:Commentz-Walter. Indeed it does, but our search isn't picking it up because
./GUIDE.md:803:PDFs are a binary format, and the text shown in the PDF may not be encoded as
./GUIDE.md:804:simple contiguous UTF-8. Namely, even passing the `-a/--text` flag to ripgrep
./GUIDE.md:805:will not make our search work.
./GUIDE.md:806:
./GUIDE.md:807:One way to fix this is to convert the PDF to plain text first. This won't work
./GUIDE.md:808:well for all PDFs, but does great in a lot of cases. (Note that the tool we
./GUIDE.md:809:use, `pdftotext`, is part of the [poppler](https://poppler.freedesktop.org)
./GUIDE.md:810:PDF rendering library.)
./GUIDE.md:811:
./GUIDE.md:812:```
./GUIDE.md:813:$ pdftotext 1995-watson.pdf > 1995-watson.txt
./GUIDE.md:814:$ rg 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.txt
./GUIDE.md:815:316:The Commentz-Walter algorithms : : : : : : : : : : : : : : :
./GUIDE.md:816:7165:4.4 The Commentz-Walter algorithms
./GUIDE.md:817:10062:in input string S , we obtain the Boyer-Moore algorithm. The Commentz-Walter algorithm
./GUIDE.md:818:17218:The Commentz-Walter algorithm (and its variants) displayed more interesting behaviour,
./GUIDE.md:819:17249:Aho-Corasick algorithms are used extensively. The Commentz-Walter algorithms are used
./GUIDE.md:820:17297: The Commentz-Walter algorithms (CW). In all versions of the CW algorithms, a common program skeleton is used with di erent shift functions. The CW algorithms are
./GUIDE.md:821:```
./GUIDE.md:822:
./GUIDE.md:823:But having to explicitly convert every file can be a pain, especially when you
./GUIDE.md:824:have a directory full of PDF files. Instead, we can use ripgrep's preprocessor
./GUIDE.md:825:feature to search the PDF. ripgrep's `--pre` flag works by taking a single
./GUIDE.md:826:command name and then executing that command for every file that it searches.
./GUIDE.md:827:ripgrep passes the file path as the first and only argument to the command and
./GUIDE.md:828:also sends the contents of the file to stdin. So let's write a simple shell
./GUIDE.md:829:script that wraps `pdftotext` in a way that conforms to this interface:
./GUIDE.md:830:
./GUIDE.md:831:```
./GUIDE.md:832:$ cat preprocess
./GUIDE.md:833:#!/bin/sh
./GUIDE.md:834:
./GUIDE.md:835:exec pdftotext - -
./GUIDE.md:836:```
./GUIDE.md:837:
./GUIDE.md:838:With `preprocess` in the same directory as `1995-watson.pdf`, we can now use it
./GUIDE.md:839:to search the PDF:
./GUIDE.md:840:
./GUIDE.md:841:```
./GUIDE.md:842:$ rg --pre ./preprocess 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf
./GUIDE.md:843:316:The Commentz-Walter algorithms : : : : : : : : : : : : : : :
./GUIDE.md:844:7165:4.4 The Commentz-Walter algorithms
./GUIDE.md:845:10062:in input string S , we obtain the Boyer-Moore algorithm. The Commentz-Walter algorithm
./GUIDE.md:846:17218:The Commentz-Walter algorithm (and its variants) displayed more interesting behaviour,
./GUIDE.md:847:17249:Aho-Corasick algorithms are used extensively. The Commentz-Walter algorithms are used
./GUIDE.md:848:17297: The Commentz-Walter algorithms (CW). In all versions of the CW algorithms, a common program skeleton is used with di erent shift functions. The CW algorithms are
./GUIDE.md:849:```
./GUIDE.md:850:
./GUIDE.md:851:Note that `preprocess` must be resolvable to a command that ripgrep can read.
./GUIDE.md:852:The simplest way to do this is to put your preprocessor command in a directory
./GUIDE.md:853:that is in your `PATH` (or equivalent), or otherwise use an absolute path.
./GUIDE.md:854:
./GUIDE.md:855:As a bonus, this turns out to be quite a bit faster than other specialized PDF
./GUIDE.md:856:grepping tools:
./GUIDE.md:857:
./GUIDE.md:858:```
./GUIDE.md:859:$ time rg --pre ./preprocess 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf -c
./GUIDE.md:860:6
./GUIDE.md:861:
./GUIDE.md:862:real    0.697
./GUIDE.md:863:user    0.684
./GUIDE.md:864:sys     0.007
./GUIDE.md:865:maxmem  16 MB
./GUIDE.md:866:faults  0
./GUIDE.md:867:
./GUIDE.md:868:$ time pdfgrep 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf -c
./GUIDE.md:869:6
./GUIDE.md:870:
./GUIDE.md:871:real    1.336
./GUIDE.md:872:user    1.310
./GUIDE.md:873:sys     0.023
./GUIDE.md:874:maxmem  16 MB
./GUIDE.md:875:faults  0
./GUIDE.md:876:```
./GUIDE.md:877:
./GUIDE.md:878:If you wind up needing to search a lot of PDFs, then ripgrep's parallelism can
./GUIDE.md:879:make the speed difference even greater.
./GUIDE.md:880:
./GUIDE.md:881:#### A more robust preprocessor
./GUIDE.md:882:
./GUIDE.md:883:One of the problems with the aforementioned preprocessor is that it will fail
./GUIDE.md:884:if you try to search a file that isn't a PDF:
./GUIDE.md:885:
./GUIDE.md:886:```
./GUIDE.md:887:$ echo foo > not-a-pdf
./GUIDE.md:888:$ rg --pre ./preprocess 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' not-a-pdf
./GUIDE.md:889:not-a-pdf: preprocessor command failed: '"./preprocess" "not-a-pdf"':
./GUIDE.md:890:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
./GUIDE.md:891:Syntax Warning: May not be a PDF file (continuing anyway)
./GUIDE.md:892:Syntax Error: Couldn't find trailer dictionary
./GUIDE.md:893:Syntax Error: Couldn't find trailer dictionary
./GUIDE.md:894:Syntax Error: Couldn't read xref table
./GUIDE.md:895:```
./GUIDE.md:896:
./GUIDE.md:897:To fix this, we can make our preprocessor script a bit more robust by only
./GUIDE.md:898:running `pdftotext` when we think the input is a non-empty PDF:
./GUIDE.md:899:
./GUIDE.md:900:```
./GUIDE.md:901:$ cat preprocessor
./GUIDE.md:902:#!/bin/sh
./GUIDE.md:903:
./GUIDE.md:904:case "$1" in
./GUIDE.md:905:*.pdf)
./GUIDE.md:906:  # The -s flag ensures that the file is non-empty.
./GUIDE.md:907:  if [ -s "$1" ]; then
./GUIDE.md:908:    exec pdftotext - -
./GUIDE.md:909:  else
./GUIDE.md:910:    exec cat
./GUIDE.md:911:  fi
./GUIDE.md:912:  ;;
./GUIDE.md:913:*)
./GUIDE.md:914:  exec cat
./GUIDE.md:915:  ;;
./GUIDE.md:916:esac
./GUIDE.md:917:```
./GUIDE.md:918:
./GUIDE.md:919:We can even extend our preprocessor to search other kinds of files. Sometimes
./GUIDE.md:920:we don't always know the file type from the file name, so we can use the `file`
./GUIDE.md:921:utility to "sniff" the type of the file based on its contents:
./GUIDE.md:922:
./GUIDE.md:923:```
./GUIDE.md:924:$ cat processor
./GUIDE.md:925:#!/bin/sh
./GUIDE.md:926:
./GUIDE.md:927:case "$1" in
./GUIDE.md:928:*.pdf)
./GUIDE.md:929:  # The -s flag ensures that the file is non-empty.
./GUIDE.md:930:  if [ -s "$1" ]; then
./GUIDE.md:931:    exec pdftotext - -
./GUIDE.md:932:  else
./GUIDE.md:933:    exec cat
./GUIDE.md:934:  fi
./GUIDE.md:935:  ;;
./GUIDE.md:936:*)
./GUIDE.md:937:  case $(file "$1") in
./GUIDE.md:938:  *Zstandard*)
./GUIDE.md:939:    exec pzstd -cdq
./GUIDE.md:940:    ;;
./GUIDE.md:941:  *)
./GUIDE.md:942:    exec cat
./GUIDE.md:943:    ;;
./GUIDE.md:944:  esac
./GUIDE.md:945:  ;;
./GUIDE.md:946:esac
./GUIDE.md:947:```
./GUIDE.md:948:
./GUIDE.md:949:#### Reducing preprocessor overhead
./GUIDE.md:950:
./GUIDE.md:951:There is one more problem with the above approach: it requires running a
./GUIDE.md:952:preprocessor for every single file that ripgrep searches. If every file needs
./GUIDE.md:953:a preprocessor, then this is OK. But if most don't, then this can substantially
./GUIDE.md:954:slow down searches because of the overhead of launching new processors. You
./GUIDE.md:955:can avoid this by telling ripgrep to only invoke the preprocessor when the file
./GUIDE.md:956:path matches a glob. For example, consider the performance difference even when
./GUIDE.md:957:searching a repository as small as ripgrep's:
./GUIDE.md:958:
./GUIDE.md:959:```
./GUIDE.md:960:$ time rg --pre pre-rg 'fn is_empty' -c
./GUIDE.md:961:crates/globset/src/lib.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:962:crates/matcher/src/lib.rs:2
./GUIDE.md:963:crates/ignore/src/overrides.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:964:crates/ignore/src/gitignore.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:965:crates/ignore/src/types.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:966:
./GUIDE.md:967:real    0.138
./GUIDE.md:968:user    0.485
./GUIDE.md:969:sys     0.209
./GUIDE.md:970:maxmem  7 MB
./GUIDE.md:971:faults  0
./GUIDE.md:972:
./GUIDE.md:973:$ time rg --pre pre-rg --pre-glob '*.pdf' 'fn is_empty' -c
./GUIDE.md:974:crates/globset/src/lib.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:975:crates/ignore/src/types.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:976:crates/ignore/src/gitignore.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:977:crates/ignore/src/overrides.rs:1
./GUIDE.md:978:crates/matcher/src/lib.rs:2

./GUIDE.md:987:
./GUIDE.md:988:### Common options
./GUIDE.md:989:
./GUIDE.md:990:ripgrep has a lot of flags. Too many to keep in your head at once. This section
./GUIDE.md:991:is intended to give you a sampling of some of the most important and frequently
./GUIDE.md:992:used options that will likely impact how you use ripgrep on a regular basis.
./GUIDE.md:993:
./GUIDE.md:994:* `-h`: Show ripgrep's condensed help output.
./GUIDE.md:995:* `--help`: Show ripgrep's longer form help output. (Nearly what you'd find in
./GUIDE.md:996:  ripgrep's man page, so pipe it into a pager!)
./GUIDE.md:997:* `-i/--ignore-case`: When searching for a pattern, ignore case differences.
./GUIDE.md:998:  That is `rg -i fast` matches `fast`, `fASt`, `FAST`, etc.
./GUIDE.md:999:* `-S/--smart-case`: This is similar to `--ignore-case`, but disables itself
./GUIDE.md:1000:  if the pattern contains any uppercase letters. Usually this flag is put into
./GUIDE.md:1001:  alias or a config file.
./GUIDE.md:1002:* `-F/--fixed-strings`: Disable regular expression matching and treat the pattern
./GUIDE.md:1003:   as a literal string.
./GUIDE.md:1004:* `-w/--word-regexp`: Require that all matches of the pattern be surrounded
./GUIDE.md:1005:  by word boundaries. That is, given `pattern`, the `--word-regexp` flag will
./GUIDE.md:1006:  cause ripgrep to behave as if `pattern` were actually
./GUIDE.md:1007:  `\b{start-half}(?:pattern)\b{end-half}`.
./GUIDE.md:1008:  (Unlike `\b`, these half-boundaries don't require a word character on one
./GUIDE.md:1009:  side. For example, `rg -w -e -2` will match `-2` in `(-2)` but `rg '\b-2\b'`
./GUIDE.md:1010:  will not.)
./GUIDE.md:1011:* `-c/--count`: Report a count of total matched lines.
./GUIDE.md:1012:* `--files`: Print the files that ripgrep *would* search, but don't actually
./GUIDE.md:1013:  search them.
./GUIDE.md:1014:* `-a/--text`: Search binary files as if they were plain text.
./GUIDE.md:1015:* `-U/--multiline`: Permit matches to span multiple lines.
./GUIDE.md:1016:* `-z/--search-zip`: Search compressed files (gzip, bzip2, lzma, xz, lz4,
./GUIDE.md:1017:  brotli, zstd). This is disabled by default.
./GUIDE.md:1018:* `-C/--context`: Show the lines surrounding a match.
./GUIDE.md:1019:* `--sort path`: Force ripgrep to sort its output by file name. (This disables
./GUIDE.md:1020:  parallelism, so it might be slower.)
./GUIDE.md:1021:* `-L/--follow`: Follow symbolic links while recursively searching.
./GUIDE.md:1022:* `-M/--max-columns`: Limit the length of lines printed by ripgrep.
./GUIDE.md:1023:* `--debug`: Shows ripgrep's debug output. This is useful for understanding
./GUIDE.md:1024:  why a particular file might be ignored from search, or what kinds of
./GUIDE.md:1025:  configuration ripgrep is loading from the environment.

./CHANGELOG.md:54:15.0.0 (2025-10-15)
./CHANGELOG.md:55:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:56:ripgrep 15 is a new major version release of ripgrep that mostly has bug fixes,
./CHANGELOG.md:57:some minor performance improvements and minor new features. Here are some
./CHANGELOG.md:58:highlights:
./CHANGELOG.md:59:
./CHANGELOG.md:60:* Several bugs around gitignore matching have been fixed. This includes
./CHANGELOG.md:61:  a commonly reported bug related to applying gitignore rules from parent
./CHANGELOG.md:62:  directories.
./CHANGELOG.md:63:* A memory usage regression when handling very large gitignore files has been
./CHANGELOG.md:64:  fixed.
./CHANGELOG.md:65:* `rg -vf file`, where `file` is empty, now matches everything.
./CHANGELOG.md:66:* The `-r/--replace` flag now works with `--json`.
./CHANGELOG.md:67:* A subset of Jujutsu (`jj`) repositories are now treated as if they were git
./CHANGELOG.md:68:  repositories. That is, ripgrep will respect `jj`'s gitignores.
./CHANGELOG.md:69:* Globs can now use nested curly braces.
./CHANGELOG.md:70:
./CHANGELOG.md:71:Platform support:
./CHANGELOG.md:72:
./CHANGELOG.md:73:* `aarch64` for Windows now has release artifacts.
./CHANGELOG.md:74:* `powerpc64` no longer has release artifacts generated for it. The CI
./CHANGELOG.md:75:  release workflow stopped working, and I didn't deem it worth my time to
./CHANGELOG.md:76:  debug it. If someone wants this and can test it, I'd be happy to add it
./CHANGELOG.md:77:  back.
./CHANGELOG.md:78:* ripgrep binaries are now compiled with full LTO enabled. You may notice
./CHANGELOG.md:79:  small performance improvements from this and a modest decrease in binary
./CHANGELOG.md:80:  size.

./CHANGELOG.md:161:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:162:This is a minor release with a bug fix for a matching bug. In particular, a bug
./CHANGELOG.md:163:was found that could cause ripgrep to ignore lines that should match. That is,
./CHANGELOG.md:164:false negatives. It is difficult to characterize the specific set of regexes
./CHANGELOG.md:165:in which this occurs as it requires multiple different optimization strategies
./CHANGELOG.md:166:to collide and produce an incorrect result. But as one reported example, in
./CHANGELOG.md:167:ripgrep, the regex `(?i:e.x|ex)` does not match `e-x` when it should. (This
./CHANGELOG.md:168:bug is a result of an inner literal optimization performed in the `grep-regex`
./CHANGELOG.md:169:crate and not in the `regex` crate.)

./CHANGELOG.md:240:14.0.0 (2023-11-26)
./CHANGELOG.md:241:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:242:ripgrep 14 is a new major version release of ripgrep that has some new
./CHANGELOG.md:243:features, performance improvements and a lot of bug fixes.
./CHANGELOG.md:244:
./CHANGELOG.md:245:The headlining feature in this release is hyperlink support. In this release,
./CHANGELOG.md:246:they are an opt-in feature but may change to an opt-out feature in the future.
./CHANGELOG.md:247:To enable them, try passing `--hyperlink-format default`. If you use [VS Code],
./CHANGELOG.md:248:then try passing `--hyperlink-format vscode`. Please [report your experience
./CHANGELOG.md:249:with hyperlinks][report-hyperlinks], positive or negative.
./CHANGELOG.md:250:
./CHANGELOG.md:251:[VS Code]: https://code.visualstudio.com/
./CHANGELOG.md:252:[report-hyperlinks]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/discussions/2611
./CHANGELOG.md:253:
./CHANGELOG.md:254:Another headlining development in this release is that it contains a rewrite
./CHANGELOG.md:255:of its regex engine. You generally shouldn't notice any changes, except for
./CHANGELOG.md:256:some searches may get faster. You can read more about the [regex engine rewrite
./CHANGELOG.md:257:on my blog][regex-internals]. Please [report your performance improvements or
./CHANGELOG.md:258:regressions that you notice][report-perf].
./CHANGELOG.md:259:
./CHANGELOG.md:260:[report-perf]: https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/discussions/2652
./CHANGELOG.md:261:
./CHANGELOG.md:262:Finally, ripgrep switched the library it uses for argument parsing. Users
./CHANGELOG.md:263:should not notice a difference in most cases (error messages have changed
./CHANGELOG.md:264:somewhat), but flag overrides should generally be more consistent. For example,
./CHANGELOG.md:265:things like `--no-ignore --ignore-vcs` work as one would expect (disables all
./CHANGELOG.md:266:filtering related to ignore rules except for rules found in version control
./CHANGELOG.md:267:systems such as `git`).
./CHANGELOG.md:268:
./CHANGELOG.md:269:[regex-internals]: https://blog.burntsushi.net/regex-internals/
./CHANGELOG.md:270:
./CHANGELOG.md:271:**BREAKING CHANGES**:
./CHANGELOG.md:272:
./CHANGELOG.md:273:* `rg -C1 -A2` used to be equivalent to `rg -A2`, but now it is equivalent to
./CHANGELOG.md:274:  `rg -B1 -A2`. That is, `-A` and `-B` no longer completely override `-C`.
./CHANGELOG.md:275:  Instead, they only partially override `-C`.
./CHANGELOG.md:276:
./CHANGELOG.md:277:Build process changes:
./CHANGELOG.md:278:
./CHANGELOG.md:279:* ripgrep's shell completions and man page are now created by running ripgrep
./CHANGELOG.md:280:with a new `--generate` flag. For example, `rg --generate man` will write a
./CHANGELOG.md:281:man page in `roff` format on stdout. The release archives have not changed.
./CHANGELOG.md:282:* The optional build dependency on `asciidoc` or `asciidoctor` has been
./CHANGELOG.md:283:dropped. Previously, it was used to produce ripgrep's man page. ripgrep now
./CHANGELOG.md:284:owns this process itself by writing `roff` directly.
./CHANGELOG.md:285:
./CHANGELOG.md:286:Performance improvements:
./CHANGELOG.md:287:
./CHANGELOG.md:288:* [PERF #1746](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1746):
./CHANGELOG.md:289:  Make some cases with inner literals faster.
./CHANGELOG.md:290:* [PERF #1760](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1760):
./CHANGELOG.md:291:  Make most searches with `\b` look-arounds (among others) much faster.
./CHANGELOG.md:292:* [PERF #2591](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/2591):
./CHANGELOG.md:293:  Parallel directory traversal now uses work stealing for faster searches.
./CHANGELOG.md:294:* [PERF #2642](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/2642):
./CHANGELOG.md:295:  Parallel directory traversal has some contention reduced.
./CHANGELOG.md:296:
./CHANGELOG.md:297:Feature enhancements:
./CHANGELOG.md:298:

./CHANGELOG.md:394:13.0.0 (2021-06-12)
./CHANGELOG.md:395:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:396:ripgrep 13 is a new major version release of ripgrep that primarily contains
./CHANGELOG.md:397:bug fixes, some performance improvements and a few minor breaking changes.
./CHANGELOG.md:398:There is also a fix for a security vulnerability on Windows
./CHANGELOG.md:399:([CVE-2021-3013](https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2021-3013)).
./CHANGELOG.md:400:
./CHANGELOG.md:401:Some highlights:
./CHANGELOG.md:402:
./CHANGELOG.md:403:A new short flag, `-.`, has been added. It is an alias for the `--hidden` flag,
./CHANGELOG.md:404:which instructs ripgrep to search hidden files and directories.
./CHANGELOG.md:405:
./CHANGELOG.md:406:ripgrep is now using a new
./CHANGELOG.md:407:[vectorized implementation of `memmem`](https://github.com/BurntSushi/memchr/pull/82),
./CHANGELOG.md:408:which accelerates many common searches. If you notice any performance
./CHANGELOG.md:409:regressions (or major improvements), I'd love to hear about them through an
./CHANGELOG.md:410:issue report!
./CHANGELOG.md:411:
./CHANGELOG.md:412:Also, for Windows users targeting MSVC, Cargo will now build fully static
./CHANGELOG.md:413:executables of ripgrep. The release binaries for ripgrep 13 have been compiled
./CHANGELOG.md:414:using this configuration.
./CHANGELOG.md:415:
./CHANGELOG.md:416:**BREAKING CHANGES**:
./CHANGELOG.md:417:
./CHANGELOG.md:418:**Binary detection output has changed slightly.**
./CHANGELOG.md:419:
./CHANGELOG.md:420:In this release, a small tweak has been made to the output format when a binary
./CHANGELOG.md:421:file is detected. Previously, it looked like this:
./CHANGELOG.md:422:
./CHANGELOG.md:423:```
./CHANGELOG.md:424:Binary file FOO matches (found "\0" byte around offset XXX)
./CHANGELOG.md:425:```
./CHANGELOG.md:426:
./CHANGELOG.md:427:Now it looks like this:
./CHANGELOG.md:428:
./CHANGELOG.md:429:```
./CHANGELOG.md:430:FOO: binary file matches (found "\0" byte around offset XXX)
./CHANGELOG.md:431:```
./CHANGELOG.md:432:
./CHANGELOG.md:433:**vimgrep output in multi-line now only prints the first line for each match.**
./CHANGELOG.md:434:
./CHANGELOG.md:435:See [issue 1866](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1866) for more
./CHANGELOG.md:436:discussion on this. Previously, every line in a match was duplicated, even
./CHANGELOG.md:437:when it spanned multiple lines. There are no changes to vimgrep output when
./CHANGELOG.md:438:multi-line mode is disabled.
./CHANGELOG.md:439:
./CHANGELOG.md:440:**In multi-line mode, --count is now equivalent to --count-matches.**
./CHANGELOG.md:441:
./CHANGELOG.md:442:This appears to match how `pcre2grep` implements `--count`. Previously, ripgrep
./CHANGELOG.md:443:would produce outright incorrect counts. Another alternative would be to simply
./CHANGELOG.md:444:count the number of lines---even if it's more than the number of matches---but
./CHANGELOG.md:445:that seems highly unintuitive.
./CHANGELOG.md:446:
./CHANGELOG.md:447:**FULL LIST OF FIXES AND IMPROVEMENTS:**
./CHANGELOG.md:448:
./CHANGELOG.md:449:Security fixes:
./CHANGELOG.md:450:

./CHANGELOG.md:452:  Fixes a security hole on Windows where running ripgrep with either the
./CHANGELOG.md:453:  `-z/--search-zip` or `--pre` flags can result in running arbitrary
./CHANGELOG.md:454:  executables from the current directory.
./CHANGELOG.md:455:* [VULN #1773](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1773):
./CHANGELOG.md:456:  This is the public facing issue tracking CVE-2021-3013. ripgrep's README
./CHANGELOG.md:457:  now contains a section describing how to report a vulnerability.

./CHANGELOG.md:728:11.0.0 (2019-04-15)
./CHANGELOG.md:729:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:730:ripgrep 11 is a new major version release of ripgrep that contains many bug
./CHANGELOG.md:731:fixes, some performance improvements and a few feature enhancements. Notably,
./CHANGELOG.md:732:ripgrep's user experience for binary file filtering has been improved. See the
./CHANGELOG.md:733:[guide's new section on binary data](GUIDE.md#binary-data) for more details.
./CHANGELOG.md:734:
./CHANGELOG.md:735:This release also marks a change in ripgrep's versioning. Where as the previous
./CHANGELOG.md:736:version was `0.10.0`, this version is `11.0.0`. Moving forward, ripgrep's
./CHANGELOG.md:737:major version will be increased a few times per year. ripgrep will continue to
./CHANGELOG.md:738:be conservative with respect to backwards compatibility, but may occasionally
./CHANGELOG.md:739:introduce breaking changes, which will always be documented in this CHANGELOG.
./CHANGELOG.md:740:See [issue 1172](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1172) for a bit
./CHANGELOG.md:741:more detail on why this versioning change was made.
./CHANGELOG.md:742:
./CHANGELOG.md:743:This release increases the **minimum supported Rust version** from 1.28.0 to
./CHANGELOG.md:744:1.34.0.
./CHANGELOG.md:745:
./CHANGELOG.md:746:**BREAKING CHANGES**:
./CHANGELOG.md:747:
./CHANGELOG.md:748:* ripgrep has tweaked its exit status codes to be more like GNU grep's. Namely,
./CHANGELOG.md:749:  if a non-fatal error occurs during a search, then ripgrep will now always
./CHANGELOG.md:750:  emit a `2` exit status code, regardless of whether a match is found or not.
./CHANGELOG.md:751:  Previously, ripgrep would only emit a `2` exit status code for a catastrophic
./CHANGELOG.md:752:  error (e.g., regex syntax error). One exception to this is if ripgrep is run
./CHANGELOG.md:753:  with `-q/--quiet`. In that case, if an error occurs and a match is found,
./CHANGELOG.md:754:  then ripgrep will exit with a `0` exit status code.
./CHANGELOG.md:755:* Supplying the `-u/--unrestricted` flag three times is now equivalent to
./CHANGELOG.md:756:  supplying `--no-ignore --hidden --binary`. Previously, `-uuu` was equivalent
./CHANGELOG.md:757:  to `--no-ignore --hidden --text`. The difference is that `--binary` disables
./CHANGELOG.md:758:  binary file filtering without potentially dumping binary data into your
./CHANGELOG.md:759:  terminal. That is, `rg -uuu foo` should now be equivalent to `grep -r foo`.
./CHANGELOG.md:760:* The `avx-accel` feature of ripgrep has been removed since it is no longer
./CHANGELOG.md:761:  necessary. All uses of AVX in ripgrep are now enabled automatically via
./CHANGELOG.md:762:  runtime CPU feature detection. The `simd-accel` feature does remain available
./CHANGELOG.md:763:  (only for enabling SIMD for transcoding), however, it does increase
./CHANGELOG.md:764:  compilation times substantially at the moment.

./CHANGELOG.md:856:0.10.0 (2018-09-07)
./CHANGELOG.md:857:===================
./CHANGELOG.md:858:This is a new minor version release of ripgrep that contains some major new
./CHANGELOG.md:859:features, a huge number of bug fixes, and is the first release based on
./CHANGELOG.md:860:libripgrep. The entirety of ripgrep's core search and printing code has been
./CHANGELOG.md:861:rewritten and generalized so that anyone can make use of it.
./CHANGELOG.md:862:
./CHANGELOG.md:863:Major new features include PCRE2 support, multi-line search and a JSON output
./CHANGELOG.md:864:format.
./CHANGELOG.md:865:
./CHANGELOG.md:866:**BREAKING CHANGES**:
./CHANGELOG.md:867:
./CHANGELOG.md:868:* The minimum version required to compile Rust has now changed to track the
./CHANGELOG.md:869:  latest stable version of Rust. Patch releases will continue to compile with
./CHANGELOG.md:870:  the same version of Rust as the previous patch release, but new minor
./CHANGELOG.md:871:  versions will use the current stable version of the Rust compile as its
./CHANGELOG.md:872:  minimum supported version.
./CHANGELOG.md:873:* The match semantics of `-w/--word-regexp` have changed slightly. They used
./CHANGELOG.md:874:  to be `\b(?:<your pattern>)\b`, but now it's
./CHANGELOG.md:875:  `(?:^|\W)(?:<your pattern>)(?:$|\W)`. This matches the behavior of GNU grep
./CHANGELOG.md:876:  and is believed to be closer to the intended semantics of the flag. See
./CHANGELOG.md:877:  [#389](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/389) for more details.

./CHANGELOG.md:941:0.9.0 (2018-08-03)
./CHANGELOG.md:942:==================
./CHANGELOG.md:943:This is a new minor version release of ripgrep that contains some minor new
./CHANGELOG.md:944:features and a panoply of bug fixes.
./CHANGELOG.md:945:
./CHANGELOG.md:946:Releases provided on Github for `x86_64` will now work on all target CPUs, and
./CHANGELOG.md:947:will also automatically take advantage of features found on modern CPUs (such
./CHANGELOG.md:948:as AVX2) for additional optimizations.
./CHANGELOG.md:949:
./CHANGELOG.md:950:This release increases the **minimum supported Rust version** from 1.20.0 to
./CHANGELOG.md:951:1.23.0.
./CHANGELOG.md:952:
./CHANGELOG.md:953:It is anticipated that the next release of ripgrep (0.10.0) will provide
./CHANGELOG.md:954:multi-line search support and a JSON output format.
./CHANGELOG.md:955:
./CHANGELOG.md:956:**BREAKING CHANGES**:
./CHANGELOG.md:957:
./CHANGELOG.md:958:* When `--count` and `--only-matching` are provided simultaneously, the
./CHANGELOG.md:959:  behavior of ripgrep is as if the `--count-matches` flag was given. That is,
./CHANGELOG.md:960:  the total number of matches is reported, where there may be multiple matches
./CHANGELOG.md:961:  per line. Previously, the behavior of ripgrep was to report the total number
./CHANGELOG.md:962:  of matching lines. (Note that this behavior diverges from the behavior of
./CHANGELOG.md:963:  GNU grep.)
./CHANGELOG.md:964:* Octal syntax is no longer supported. ripgrep previously accepted expressions
./CHANGELOG.md:965:  like `\1` as syntax for matching `U+0001`, but ripgrep will now report an
./CHANGELOG.md:966:  error instead.
./CHANGELOG.md:967:* The `--line-number-width` flag has been removed. Its functionality was not
./CHANGELOG.md:968:  carefully considered with all ripgrep output formats.
./CHANGELOG.md:969:  See [#795](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/795) for more
./CHANGELOG.md:970:  details.
